question: Can a neural network learn task-dependent features in a rich regime yet end at the same predictor as kernel regression with its final, data-dependent neural tangent kernel?

key_findings.claim: The paper identifies a sufficient two-phase mechanism for a final-NTK kernel solution.
key_findings.evidence: If an initially small NTK changes its eigenstructure before predictions move, then subsequently grows only by a scalar factor, the small-initialization limit of gradient flow yields kernel regression using the final rather than initial NTK.

anchors.section: 2 Silent Alignment and Approximate Kernel Solution

key_findings.claim: Two-layer linear networks on whitened data analytically realize the mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: Around the small zero-weight saddle, a task-aligned rank-one kernel component emerges on time scale 1/s while loss stays high; scale growth and fitting begin only near s^{-1} log(s/sigma^2), creating asymptotic separation as initialization shrinks.

key_findings.claim: Deep linear networks retain task-aligned final kernels, but the clean time-scale argument weakens beyond depth two.
key_findings.evidence: Balance conservation yields a rank-one spike whose alignment strength grows with depth; for depth at least three, alignment and half-loss times share the same sigma power-law scaling, so separation is empirical rather than parametrically guaranteed.

key_findings.claim: Whitened nonlinear networks show final-NTK agreement in controlled experiments.
key_findings.evidence: Binary MNIST/CIFAR MLPs and a small-data Wide-ResNet exhibit early label alignment, later norm/loss growth, and much stronger correlation between trained predictions and final-NTK regression than with the initial NTK.

anchors.section: 5 Silent Alignment on Real Data and ReLU Nets

key_findings.claim: Input anisotropy is a demonstrated counterexample to the simple mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: For unwhitened linear data the kernel first aligns to Sigma beta and must realign later; on partially whitened CIFAR, label alignment continues while loss falls and final-NTK predictions diverge increasingly from the trained network.

key_findings.claim: Final-NTK equivalence is retrospective, not a reduction of neural training to a fixed kernel method.
key_findings.evidence: The final kernel is computed only after label-dependent feature learning has occurred and can encode the task solution; the experiments compare predictions after training, without showing that the kernel or generalization can be predicted from initialization and data beforehand.

method.core_idea: Integrate gradient-flow prediction dynamics through the evolving NTK and find conditions under which all meaningful eigenstructure is learned before output fitting, leaving a final phase equivalent to scalar-rescaled kernel descent.
method.mechanism: Analyze balanced homogeneous linear networks at small initialization, solve two-layer alignment and scale dynamics, extend the final-kernel form through layer-balance invariants, and compare trained outputs with initial- and final-NTK regression on whitened and anisotropic image data.
assumptions: Training follows gradient flow with squared loss in the core theorem.
Initialization is sufficiently small for leading-order balance and saddle dynamics.
Inputs are whitened or approximately isotropic.
The kernel's eigenstructure stabilizes before loss decreases appreciably.
Empirical finite-width NTKs are estimated accurately enough for post-training kernel regression.

techniques.role: Expresses the final predictor as an integral over the complete kernel trajectory.
Separates label-direction learning from later scalar spectral growth.
Constrains small-initialized deep linear weights to low-rank aligned structure.
Tests whether a post-training kernel reproduces network predictions.
Intervenes on input anisotropy to reveal when late realignment breaks equivalence.

evaluations.setting: Two-layer linear teacher-student regression with whitened inputs.
evaluations.metric: Kernel alignment, kernel norm, loss, and analytic trajectory agreement.
evaluations.result: Alignment precedes loss by a logarithmically expanding interval as initialization shrinks, and the final kernel has a task-direction spike.
evaluations.baseline: Initial NTK and exact/numerical gradient-flow dynamics.

evaluations.setting: Deep linear networks over initialization scale and depth.
evaluations.metric: Time to half alignment, time to half loss, and final alignment.
evaluations.result: Alignment occurs first empirically and final task alignment strengthens with depth, although both times have the same small-sigma scaling beyond depth two.
evaluations.baseline: Derived power-law time scaling and shallower networks.

evaluations.setting: Whitened binary MNIST and CIFAR-10 with ReLU/Tanh MLPs.
evaluations.metric: Label-kernel alignment and correlation of trained versus kernel-regression predictions.
evaluations.result: Final NTKs approximate trained functions much better than initial NTKs under small initialization.
evaluations.baseline: Kernel regression using the initial NTK.

evaluations.setting: Wide-ResNet on 100 whitened binary CIFAR-10 examples.
evaluations.metric: Kernel alignment/norm, loss, and prediction correlation.
evaluations.result: A qualitative silent-alignment signature persists under Adam in the small-data setup.
evaluations.baseline: Initial versus final empirical NTK predictors.

evaluations.metric: Alignment trajectory, loss, test error, and final-NTK prediction agreement.
evaluations.result: Greater anisotropy produces continuing kernel rotation and degrades final-NTK equivalence.
evaluations.baseline: Fully or more strongly whitened inputs.

limitations: The exact theory concerns linear homogeneous networks, squared loss, gradient flow, small initialization, and whitened data.
Reviewer inference: nonlinear evidence uses binary tasks, small sample sizes, whitening, and unusually small learning rates rather than standard full-scale training.
Reviewer inference: final-NTK agreement is a post hoc descriptive test because computing the kernel requires the trained network.
Reviewer inference: correlation plots do not establish equality, calibration, or identical generalization off the measured test set.
Reviewer inference: for depth at least three the claimed phases lack a parameterically separated time scale.
Reviewer inference: the work does not show silent alignment is necessary; other evolving-kernel paths can produce a final-kernel solution.
failure_modes: Natural covariance anisotropy forces late kernel rotation during loss reduction.
Normalization layers, biases, nonhomogeneous activations, or cross-entropy invalidate balance and scale assumptions.
Finite initialization makes early predictions large enough that alignment and fitting are inseparable.
Multiple teacher modes learn on overlapping time scales and prevent a single frozen eigenbasis.
The final empirical NTK is singular or poorly conditioned, making interpolation unstable.
A final-NTK predictor matches sampled outputs but differs under distribution shift or adversarial directions.
reusable_insights: Feature learning and representability by a kernel machine are not mutually exclusive when the kernel itself is learned from labels.
Kernel direction, eigenvalues, and overall norm should be tracked separately over time.
Whitening is a mechanistic intervention, not a harmless preprocessing detail, in feature-learning theory.
A post-training surrogate needs prospective or counterfactual tests before it can explain generalization.
open_questions: Which standard architectures and losses exhibit silent alignment without explicit whitening?
Can the final data-dependent kernel be predicted from training data without running the full neural optimization?
Are there finite-width error bounds linking final-NTK regression to the trained nonlinear predictor?
How do normalization, residual scaling, momentum, and cross-entropy alter the phase ordering?
Does final-NTK equivalence persist under natural distribution shift and multiclass full-data training?

competitive_landscape.title: Kernel and Rich Regimes in Overparametrized Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Woodworth et al. show initialization scale controls lazy-to-rich implicit bias in homogeneous models; silent alignment identifies a special rich trajectory that nevertheless ends as regression with a learned final kernel.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Regularization via Neural Feature Alignment
competitive_landscape.difference: Baratin et al. measure tangent-feature alignment along training and motivate a path-class complexity; the reviewed paper derives a two-phase mechanism and an explicit final-kernel representer result.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep learning versus kernel learning: an empirical study of loss landscape geometry and the time evolution of the Neural Tangent Kernel
competitive_landscape.difference: Fort et al. already observe rapid early NTK change followed by a final-NTK approximation; the reviewed work supplies an analytic small-initialization explanation in linear networks.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Networks can Learn Representations with Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Damian et al. exhibit targets efficiently learned by neural representation learning but not fixed kernels; silent alignment is compatible because its final kernel is label- and data-dependent rather than fixed before training.

competitive_landscape.title: Exact and Rich Feature Learning Dynamics of Two-Layer Linear Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Huang et al. characterize precise nonlinear trajectories of feature alignment and network weights, extending beyond the reviewed paper's deliberately transparent leading-order two-layer derivation.

competitive_landscape.title: Three Mechanisms of Feature Learning in an Analytically Solvable Model
competitive_landscape.difference: This solvable-model work distinguishes alignment, disalignment, and rescaling mechanisms; silent alignment combines early alignment with later rescaling and is therefore one special feature-learning pattern.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Rich feature learning can culminate in a kernel-regression solution through silent alignment of an initially small NTK followed by pure scale growth.
novelty_assessment.evidence: A general sufficient-condition theorem, analytic linear-network dynamics, deep balance formulas, and controlled nonlinear image experiments support the mechanism while anisotropy provides a falsifying boundary case.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The reconciliation of rich learning with a final learned-kernel predictor is conceptually sharp, although rapid early NTK alignment was observed previously. Scope is narrow and retrospective; later work gives exact dynamics and a wider taxonomy of feature-learning mechanisms.
